messages.subject: identification SEM model
parts:
Can someone explain to me how I calculate the non-redundant parameters? I read everywhere that you calculate this by p (p + 1) / 2,
but do you have to do this per latent variable or in total or with aptitude and social support combined (since they covary).

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: identification SEM model
parts:
Michelle--
     Counting DF can be tricky, because you will eitehr have some loadings fixed or else some factor variances fixed, in order to "scale" each factor. DF need to be counted for the whole model, though you also need to know that each part is identified. Remember that DF >+ 0 is only a necessary condition for identification--it is not sufficient.
     Long ago I suggested a little algorithm for hand-counting DF (see attached). For your model, it would work like this:
The  model has 16 observed variables (p = 16), so the number of unique elements in the covariance matrix is:

p*(p+1) / 2 = 136

Then subtract 2p covering observed variable residual variances, loadings and factor variances:

-2p = -32

Subtract 1 for each free covariance (I count 5)

-5

Subtract 1 for every free path between factors (I count 7)

-7

So DF should be 136 - 32 - 5 - 7 = 92.

     I do not know of any simple rule to tell you whether your model with residual covariances for all 4 indicators of previous happiness and happiness will be identified. There was a Bollen and Davis paper from back in the 1980s, but I found that rule itself complicated. Look out for signs of underidentification in your output. It may very well depends on your particular parameter estimates.

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: identification SEM model
parts:
Michelle,
   Be careful if you are using fixed.x estimation (possibly by default) because that changes the calculation for the number of unique moments available for df.  Let p be the number of observed variables and x be the number of exogenous observed variables.  If you are only analyzing covariances (not means) then you can compute the number of unique moments as follows.

myMomentCount <- function(p, x=NULL){
  count <- (p * (p + 1)) / 2
  if(!is.null(x)){
    discount <- (x * (x + 1)) / 2
    count <- count  - discount
  }
  return(count)
}
Enter code here...

So, if you are not using fixed.x, then you get 136 moments from 16 variables, as you noted.  Suppose that you had 4 exogenous variables (your model has none).  These 4 variables produce 10 moments.  So, for the purposes of DF, you would count 126 = 136 - 10 if using fixed.x.

I also recommend the following article:
Rigdon, E. E. (1995).  A necessary and sufficient identification rule for structural models estimated in practice.  Multivariate Behavioral Research, 30, 359-383.

Keith
